concepts.title: Concluding Remarks on Writing
concepts.one_liner: Good writing requires significant time for rewriting, often making structural and clarity improvements more valuable than last-minute result tweaks.
concepts.content: The approaches to writing and editing described previously all take time, as good writing involves significant rewriting. The final days before a paper submission deadline are often better spent improving the structure, presentation, and clarity of the paper rather than attempting to obtain last-minute improvements to the results.
concepts.motivation_md: Authors often over-prioritize data over presentation. This concept emphasizes that a well-communicated result is more likely to be accepted and understood than a slightly better result that is poorly explained.

concepts.title: The Importance of Giving Good Talks
concepts.one_liner: The ability to give a good talk is a critical skill that helps researchers and engineers successfully communicate their work.
concepts.content: Giving good talks is important for students, researchers, and engineers. While one might think the work itself is all that counts, the ability to give a good talk is like having a big serve in tennis; it doesn't win the game alone, but it is a hallmark of the best players. This chapter provides heuristics for giving effective talks, though readers are encouraged to access other sources to find the tips that work best for them.
concepts.motivation_md: Technical work has little impact if it cannot be communicated effectively. Mastering public speaking ensures that your ideas reach and influence your audience.

key_passage.text: Giving good talks is important for people who use the material of this book--for students, researchers, and engineers.

motivation.text: One might think, "It is the work itself that really counts. Giving a talk about it is secondary." But the ability to give a good talk is like having a big serve in tennis---by itself, it doesn't win the game for you, but it sure helps.

concepts.title: Connecting with the audience
concepts.one_liner: Connecting with the audience by sharing excitement and showing genuine interest in the topic is essential for a successful technical presentation.
concepts.content: Connecting with the audience is a vital component of scientific presentations. Actor Alan Alda has noted that scientific speaking improves significantly when presenters engage in improvisational theater exercises, which prime them to connect with others and make their talks sparkle. An audience generally wants three things from a technical talk: (a) for the presentation to follow a logical sequence that makes sense, (b) to learn a few new things, and (c) to connect with the speaker and share their excitement for the topic. Ultimately, the audience wants to watch you love something.
concepts.motivation_md: Technical talks often fail not because of poor data, but because the speaker fails to engage the audience. Establishing a human connection ensures the audience remains attentive and receptive to the information being shared.
concepts.recap_md: - Audiences value logical flow and the opportunity to learn new things.

key_passage.text: To connect with the speaker, to share their excitement for the topic. They want to watch you love something!

motivation.text: Alda noted the improvement in scientific speaking of volunteers after they engaged in improvisational theater exercises. After the exercises, the volunteers were primed to engage and connect with others, and their scientific talks sparkled.

concepts.title: Ending a presentation
concepts.one_liner: Ending a presentation with a clear "Thank you" signals the audience to applaud and provides a professional transition to the Q&A session.
concepts.content: How you end a talk significantly impacts the audience's response. A common but awkward method is to end by asking, "Are there any questions?" This often leaves the audience confused about whether to applaud or ask a question, resulting in scattered applause. A better approach is to close with "Thank you," which clearly signals the time for applause; you can then ask for questions afterward. However, some experts, like Patrick Winston, disagree with ending with "thank you," arguing it implies the audience did the speaker a favor. Winston preferred to conclude by reminding the audience how he fulfilled his initial promise regarding what they would learn.
concepts.motivation_md: A clear ending prevents the awkward silence or confusion that occurs when an audience isn't sure if a presentation has concluded, ensuring the talk ends on a high note.
concepts.recap_md: - Closing with "Thank you" provides a clear cue for audience applause.

key_passage.text: Better is to close with "Thank you." The audience then knows it's their time to applaud, and they will.

question.text: How should you end your talk?

motivation.text: A common, but awkward, way is to end by asking, "Are there any questions?" The audience wants to clap at the end of a talk, but with that ending, they don't know whether to applaud or to ask a question, and they're likely to give only scattered applause.

concepts.title: Taxonomy of Talks
concepts.one_liner: Technical talks range in length and audience familiarity, requiring material that prevents the uninitiated from being lost while still engaging those familiar with the topic.
concepts.content: There are different kinds of talks, ranging from 3-minute "fast-forward" sessions to hour-long keynote addresses. You may be one of many speakers at a conference or visit a university for a special seminar; for example, @MITFacultyJobTalks2022 provides tips for faculty job talks. Audiences often have a wide range of familiarity with your topic, so it is essential to include material that prevents the uninitiated from being lost. Even experts appreciate hearing foundational material presented clearly and well.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the variety of talk formats and audience backgrounds helps speakers tailor their material so that everyone, from novices to experts, remains engaged and informed.
concepts.recap_md: - Technical talks range from short advertisements to long keynote addresses. - Audiences often have diverse levels of expertise, requiring material that accommodates both novices and experts.

key_passage.text: There are different kinds of talks. Conference and workshop talks may range in length between 3 minutes for a "fast-forward" talk to 45 or 60 minutes for a keynote address.

motivation.text: It is very often the case that the audience will have a wide range of familiarity with the work and topic that you will present about. So you will to include material to let the uninitiated not be lost.

concepts.title: Very Short Talks
concepts.one_liner: Short talks are often advertisements designed to persuade the listener to read a paper or listen to a longer version of the talk by conveying the main idea and excitement.
concepts.content: Short talks (2–10 minutes) are often advertisements designed to persuade the listener to read a paper or attend a longer version of the talk. Rather than conveying many details, aim to have the audience remember the main idea and share your excitement. For five-minute presentations, cover these points: 1. What problem did you address? 2. Why is it interesting? 3. Why is it hard? 4. What was the key to your approach? 5. How well did it work? This structure is applicable to other short talks, and because they are brief, you should practice them from start to finish several times.
concepts.motivation_md: Short time limits require a focused strategy to capture interest quickly without overwhelming the audience with technical minutiae.
concepts.recap_md: - Focus on the main idea and your excitement rather than technical details. - Use a five-point structure: problem, interest, difficulty, approach, and results. - Practice the entire talk multiple times since the duration is short.

key_passage.text: Short talks are often advertisements, designed to persuade the listener to read your paper, or to listen to a longer version of the talk. Rather than trying to convey many details about your work, you should aim to have the audience remember the main idea behind your work, and to share your excitement about the work.

concepts.title: Talk Preparation
concepts.one_liner: The keys to a good talk and overcoming nerves are preparation and practice, including thinking through the narrative story and visiting the speaking venue in advance.
concepts.content: (see figure: The key to a good talk: preparation and practice.) The keys to a good talk and overcoming nerves are preparation and practice. While it is usually better to speak from notes than a script to keep the audience engaged, writing a script can help those speaking in a non-native language or navigating difficult sections. Identifying the "story" or narrative flow is crucial; reorder the presentation if necessary to create a better connection between parts. If possible, visit the room beforehand to check the lectern, identify sightline issues, and plan how to position yourself to engage the audience.
concepts.motivation_md: Preparation reduces anxiety and ensures a coherent narrative, while physical site visits prevent logistical issues from distracting the speaker or audience.
concepts.recap_md: - Practice and prepare thoroughly to manage nerves and ensure a smooth delivery. - Focus on the narrative "story" to help the audience follow the logical flow of the presentation. - Visit the speaking venue in advance to plan positioning and audience engagement.

motivation.text: We believe the keys to both a good talk and to overcoming nerves are the same: prepare and practice.

concepts.title: Managing Nervousness
concepts.one_liner: Nervousness is a common experience for public speakers that can be reduced through thorough preparation and a deep understanding of the lecture material.
concepts.content: Public speaking can be stressful, and many speakers find the hours before a presentation to be particularly nerve-wracking. This time is often spent reviewing the talk to improve it or preparing for potential questions. However, thorough preparation and a deep mastery of the lecture material are effective ways to reduce this stress.
concepts.motivation_md: Acknowledging that nervousness is normal helps speakers focus on actionable strategies, like preparation, to manage their anxiety.
concepts.recap_md: - Nervousness is a common experience even for seasoned public speakers. - Increasing preparation and mastery of the material directly reduces stress levels.

key_passage.text: The more I prepare, and the better I know the lecture material, the less stressed I am.

motivation.text: I still find the hours before giving a presentation to be stressful. I'm always reviewing my talk to try to improve it or to track down the answers to questions I think someone might ask me.

concepts.title: Nervousness in public speaking
concepts.one_liner: Practicing a talk aloud and focusing on the goal of conveying information to the audience are effective strategies for managing public speaking anxiety.
concepts.content: A great cure for nervousness is to practice the talk aloud, both alone and in front of friends. To calm your nerves, remind yourself that the audience is there to hear the information rather than to see you; your primary task is simply to convey that information. As Dr. Rob Gilbert @Gilbert noted, it is acceptable to have butterflies in your stomach as long as you get them to fly in formation.
concepts.motivation_md: These techniques provide practical mental shifts and behavioral habits to transform nervous energy into a productive performance.
concepts.recap_md: - Practice the talk aloud multiple times to build confidence and fluency. - Shift your focus from self-consciousness to the goal of conveying information to the audience.

key_passage.text: It's all right to have butterflies in your stomach. Your job is to get them to fly in formation.

concepts.title: Engaging the audience
concepts.one_liner: To engage a distracted audience, speakers should use active techniques such as asking questions or posing sub-problems for the listeners to solve.
concepts.content: Audiences are often distracted by social media, email, or other tasks, so speakers must prepare specifically to engage them. One technique is to ask the audience questions, as suggested by Patrick Winston @WinstonSpeaks. Bill Hoogterp @Hoogterp suggests giving the audience "something to work on" while they listen, such as posing a sub-problem you faced. This draws them in and makes them more receptive to your eventual solution.
concepts.motivation_md: Since modern audiences are easily distracted, speakers need active strategies to pull listeners back into the presentation and keep them mentally involved.
concepts.recap_md: - Use questions to break the audience's passive state and increase engagement. - Pose sub-problems to give the audience a mental task that makes them more receptive to your solutions.

key_passage.text: The audience is like a sheep dog, always wanting to be working. Give the audience something to work on while they're listening to you.

question.text: Can you think of a technique to get the audience more engaged in the talk?

motivation.text: In reality, on most every speaking situation, your audience is a collection of people who are checking their social media or email, looking on their laptops for other talks to attend, or are hungry or fidgety. We have to practise and prepare in order to engage the audience.

concepts.title: Layering a talk
concepts.one_liner: Layering a talk with verbal transitions and dynamic delivery helps both attentive and distracted listeners follow the presentation's structure and main points.
concepts.content: Layering a talk involves providing verbal cues and transitions between sections to help the audience follow the structure. This keeps even distracted listeners from being lost, as they can hear "verbal headings" like: "The probability of an observation has three terms to it. $\ldots$ blah blah $\ldots$ So that gives us the objective function we want to optimize. Now, how do we find the optimal value?" Additionally, using verbal dynamics—variations in speed or intensity—and showing genuine excitement about the work makes the talk easier and more enjoyable to follow.
concepts.motivation_md: Layering provides a roadmap for the audience, ensuring that even if they tune out momentarily, they can easily re-orient themselves when the speaker signals a new section.
concepts.recap_md: - Use verbal cues and transitions to act as "headings" that guide the audience through the talk's structure. - Employ verbal dynamics and show genuine enthusiasm to maintain audience interest.

key_passage.text: It's often easier for the audience to listen to your talk if you layer it---provide verbal cues for new concepts and transitions between sections of the talk.

motivation.text: This helps even the attentive listener to follow the structure of your talk. It keeps the distracted listener from being completely lost.

concepts.title: Using competing conjectures in presentations
concepts.one_liner: Setting up a "fight" between competing conjectures creates anticipation and helps the audience engage with the experimental results that reveal the winning theory.
concepts.content: Audiences enjoy a "good fight," which can be staged by setting up a conflict between two competing conjectures @Adelson95. For example, you might contrast the flat earth theory, which predicts ships appear as small versions of the complete ship (see figure: The appearance of ships approaching a port, from the flat-earth theory.), with the round earth theory, which predicts the sails appear first (see figure: Their appearance as predicted by the round-earth theory.). (see figure: The experimental evidence: a photograph of ships approaching a port.) Showing the experimental evidence reveals the winning theory and satisfies the audience's anticipation, as illustrated by the evidence in @mnsomero.
concepts.motivation_md: Framing scientific or technical results as a resolution to a conflict makes the presentation more dramatic and memorable for the audience.
concepts.recap_md: - Frame your research as a "fight" between competing theories to build narrative tension. - Use visual evidence to demonstrate which conjecture is supported by the data.

key_passage.text: You can set up a fight between two competing conjectures. For example, you might say, "The flat earth theory predicts that ships will appear on the horizon as small versions of the complete ship. Under that theory, you'd expect approaching ships to appear as in fig-boats-a. Conversely, the round earth theory predicts that the top of the sails will appear first, then gradually the rest of the ship below it, resulting in approaching ships looking as in fig-boats-b.

motivation.text: the audience loves to watch a good fight
